## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 51 (*Surāpāna sikkhāpada*, "Drinking alcohol") sets forth the monastic rule prohibiting Buddhist monks from drinking intoxicants (*surā* and *meraya*); any monk who consumes alcohol commits an offense of expiation requiring confession (*pācittiya*) [SuttaCentral; Bapat 1956]. The origin narrative (*nidāna*) is situated at Kosambī: after the Venerable Sāgata exercised his mastery of the fire element to subdue a dangerous fire-dragon at Amba Ford, the lay supporters of Kosambī, prompted by the group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā*), offered him an intoxicating brew called *kāpotikā*; Sāgata drank it, collapsed in a drunken stupor at the monastery gate, and could no longer show deference to the Buddha, which prompted the Buddha to promulgate the training rule [Bodhi 2012; Vinayamukha Vol. 3 1983]. In Theravāda Vinaya analysis, the transgression is classified as *acittaka*, meaning liability does not require deliberate mental intention [Vinayamukha Vol. 1 1969]. The precept is later central to the Second Buddhist Council controversies over the ten illicit practices (*dasa vatthūni*), where the practice of *jalogim-pātum*—drinking unfermented or fermenting palm juice that has not fully turned to toddy—was judged impermissible under Pācittiya 51 [Bapat 1956; Sarao and Long 2017; Dutt 1978; Vinayamukha Vol. 3 1983].
Within the Pali canon, this rule directly corresponds to Bhikkhunī Pācittiya 132 [SuttaCentral; Clarke 2009]. SuttaCentral records full parallels across the Vinaya literature of all early Buddhist schools, including the Prātimokṣa and Vibhaṅga recensions of the Sarvāstivāda (Pc 79), Mūlasarvāstivāda (Pc 79), Mahīśāsaka (Pc 57), Mahāsāṃghika and Lokottaravāda (Pc 76), and Dharmaguptaka (Pc 51), as well as corresponding rules for nuns across multiple traditions [SuttaCentral]. SuttaCentral also notes a resemblance to the council account in the *Sattasatikakkhandhaka* (Kd 22) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches extensive Pali-internal text reuse, particularly with Vinaya Khandhaka texts such as the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), and *Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka* (Kd 15), as well as several Saṁyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāya passages [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus include Sanskrit witnesses such as Jayarakṣita’s *Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā*, the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and the *Divyāvadāna*, along with Tibetan commentary (*Pratimokṣasūtrapaddhati*) and the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* [DharmaNexus].
